Both integrate changes from one branch into another. Different history shape.

## Merge

```
main:    A--B--C--M
                 /
feat:    D--E--F
```

`M` = merge commit. Preserves full history. Shows exactly what happened and when.

**Use when:**
- Feature branch done, merging to `main`
- Want preserve true history
- Team branch (others pull from it)
- Open source PR

**Tradeoffs:**
- ✅ Non-destructive, safe, accurate
- ❌ Noisy history with many branches

---

## Rebase

```
main:    A--B--C
feat:           D'--E'--F'
```

Replay feat commits on top of main. Linear history. `D'` = rewritten commit (new SHA).

**Use when:**
- Updating feature branch with latest `main`
- Want clean linear history before merge
- Solo branch nobody else uses

**Tradeoffs:**
- ✅ Clean history, easy `git log`, bisect works well
- ❌ Rewrites commits → **force push required** → destroys shared branch history

---

## Golden Rule

> **Never rebase public/shared branch.**

Rebase = rewrite history. Others have old SHAs. Chaos follow.

---

## Quick Decision

| Situation | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| Merge feature → main | Merge (or squash merge) |
| Update feat with latest main | Rebase |
| Shared branch | Merge only |
| Clean up local commits before PR | Rebase |
| Public repo main branch | Merge only |

---

**Common flow:**
```bash
git checkout feat
git rebase main      # keep feat fresh, linear
# ... done with feat ...
git checkout main
git merge feat       # fast-forward or merge commit
```

Rebase to stay current. Merge to integrate.
